what: precedent rules for motionmaxxing: beat role, content, mechanic, rule in our own words. Study-derived and model-decoded: unverified; look at the cited M-moment before relying on it and never let a row outrank a measured number in references/.

ids.PL####: rule decoded from a human-made reference film (opaque film id f-xxxxxxxx = sha1(original name)[:8]; no copy, frames or brand names)
ids.PM###: one of the 53 HyperFrames study moments (M### = the measured recreation cited in references/): role, mechanic, why
ids.PR-Xnn: designer rule (WHEN/DO/BECAUSE with numbers) distilled from 53 measured recreations; evidence moments listed

rule: When the opening VO is a setup phrase leading into a key noun, type it word-per-line at label size and dim each word once spoken, so the payoff noun can arrive at full scale.
When a single noun is the subject of the entire film, set it larger than the frame and track across it so it takes 2+ seconds to read, ending on a coloured element the next shot can match.
When the VO states a trend ('growing', 'more'), do not type the word; show a count of simple objects increasing, spawned from the last shot's accent shape.
When the script gives a vague large quantity ('thousands', 'millions'), fill the frame with identical tiny units and cut a quiet band for a small caption, rather than showing a number.
Right before a 'but/except' pivot, collapse the busy previous frame to a single centred element for half a second.
When the script questions a buzzword, frame that word in accent-coloured brackets and let the rest of the sentence type inside them; drop the conjunction.
When the script describes something invisible (drop-off, churn), reuse the film's established unit (dot = person) and show the gap as empty/hollow units, with only the key noun in type.
When the script dismisses a metric as 'just a number', show the number small and ticking, surrounded by larger units of what it summarises, instead of making it heroic.
When the VO lists manual workflow steps, give each step a single literal UI control that morphs out of the previous shape at the same centre point.
When a sequence of steps leads to an output, make the previous step's object the first building block of the next and pull the camera back as it accumulates.
When the VO names a small count (two to five things), show exactly that many identical containers side by side.
When the script says information is stale, outdated or dead, desaturate the finished visual to grey on that exact word.
At the pivot from 'stale/manual' to 'live', cut to large, continuously updating values that bleed off frame, set against the frozen grey of the previous shot.
When the VO has a deliberate hesitation before the answer ('well...', 'so...'), set that single word giant with an ellipsis and hold it, then cut small for the answer.
When the answer to a big question is short and confident, cut from giant to small type with lots of empty space; understatement reads as confidence.
When the VO speaks the tagline over the end card, show only the logo small and still; do not type the tagline too.

When a title is too long to open big, start the write-on at hero scale on its first word and pull the camera back as characters arrive, so frame 1 is legible and the title ends at comfortable reading size.
When a single line outgrows the frame, lock the write head at a fixed screen position and scroll the line past it, letting earlier words bleed off the edge instead of scaling the type down.
When moving from a headline to a tagline, insert a brief empty container (field, frame, card) with a cursor so the audience's eye is centred and waiting before the words arrive.
When a secondary line follows a hero title, drop it to about a third of the title's size and give it a container, keeping the same reveal cadence so hierarchy changes but voice does not.

When the film will reframe a dry category (finance, data) as human, open on that category's most recognisable glyph (a bar chart) drawn as soft primitives, and make it wordless so the later morph is the reveal.
When an abstract shape must become a character, keep its colour and cap detail and change only proportion and gait, so the viewer recognises it as the same object now alive.
When the hook is an everyday analogy, set it small and split the sentence around the animated metaphor so image and words are read as one line.
When a metaphor sequence changes idea, collapse the old glyph to a point and expand the new one from that same point, so the change reads as cause and effect, not a cut.
When a line claims effortlessness, remove an element (a frame, a ring, a UI chrome) as the line lands rather than adding one.
When the script pivots from metaphor to the real subject, drop every illustration and show the pivot line alone so the subject word lands in silence.
When a line must hand off to a product symbol, morph each word into one unit of the next shape in reading order, keeping the count, instead of fading text out.
When introducing an AI agent, pass through a recognisable 'thinking' state (orbiting dots, spinner) before its face appears so its arrival feels like it woke up.
When the product is a character, give its birth one moment of material richness (gloss, gradient) then settle it into the flat brand style so it can be reused as an icon.
When cutting from a brand character to the product, keep the character visible inside the UI (as avatar/icon) so the cut reads as the character moving into its job.
When typing a prompt into real UI, punch in 2–3× and let the camera follow the caret so the newest character stays in one place; write a specific, relatable prompt rather than a generic one.
When there is dead time between an action and the product's response, fill it with a small character or state animation rather than a hold or a spinner.
When proving an AI's intelligence, stream a specific, numbers-rich answer word by word at true UI scale; its specificity matters more than the viewer reading every word.
When a demo is a back-and-forth, repeat identical framing for each user turn so the loop is legible through repetition.
When the benefit line pays off the opening analogy, set it in exactly the same style and position as the hook line and duck the sound under it.
When revealing the full product dashboard at the end of a flat-graphic film, grow it out of the background colour and frame it with a single soft photo to add warmth without competing.
When a demo makes a promise ('I'll remind you'), show the follow-through later as a real notification entering the top of a list, so the story closes on proof.
When closing a calm film, end on a softly phrased line in the recurring lone-line style before the logo, not on a hard CTA.
When a film has been continuously morphing, end with a hard cut to a dead-still logo; the stillness itself is the full stop.
When the brand's strongest asset is its app icon, open on the icon tile itself at extreme, cropped scale and snap it to rest size within ~0.3s.
When a film is a single continuous take, give it one tiny secondary character (a dot/ball) that chases the hero, so every move has a cause and the eye always knows where to look.
When you need to change an object's colour or content mid-move, hide the swap inside the frame of peak motion blur rather than cross-fading it.
When the brand mark arrives after a chaotic motion build, land it with an impact (ring/shockwave), then hold it perfectly still for ~0.6s with a single glint.
When moving from brand mark to product UI, morph the logo container into the first UI element (shrink → blank → widen) instead of cutting.
When product context (map, feed, grid) is needed behind a hero UI element, keep it under ~25% opacity with a radial fade so it reads as place, not content.
When showing a user typing a query, render the in-progress text in the brand accent and settle it to neutral when the input is complete.
When showing search results, grow them out of the search element and stagger exactly three items ~2 frames apart.
When the next scene switches to a new colour field, seed that colour as a small UI state (hover/selection tint) in the preceding shot.
When changing scene in a one-take film, whip in the direction your guide object is already travelling.
When a key word must stay readable while its object is in motion, keep the object near-centre and move the environment (streaks, background) instead.
When ending a physical one-take, land the last object in a real context (map, table, hand) and pull back to a small, still composition held ≥1s.
When the logo mark will reappear later as a UI element, open on the mark alone for about a second so the viewer learns its shape.
When the brand mark doubles as the product's in-app icon, reveal the lockup small and then detach the mark and move it, so the eye follows it into the product.
When moving from logo to product, fly the logo mark into its real position in the UI instead of cutting.
When a film has no VO and the product is prompt-driven, crop to the input so the typed prompt reads as the headline.
When the demo hinges on one click, crop until the target control is the only saturated element in frame and hold on the click for 2+ seconds.
When showing an agent working, cascade real log rows at unreadable-but-plausible size and let only the success state carry colour.
When a silent product demo reaches a milestone, grow a dark UI element (tooltip, chip) to full frame and set a 2–4 word result caption on it for about a second.
After a 'done/ready' caption, show the result inside a physical device with a pull-back so the output feels real.
When a silent film starts a new feature section, announce it with an icon-first chip caption styled like the product UI.
When a caption line is two ideas, split it across two cards with inverted backgrounds and keep one central shape constant across the inversion.
When showing integrations, push in until the partner logos are recognisable; the logos are the proof, not the page layout.
When one dialog matters on a busy screen, blur the rest of the UI instead of adding highlights or arrows.
When the UI action is 'connect/pair a device', answer the click with that device rotating in from edge-on.
When the film already used a device mockup, put the end lockup on that same device's screen instead of a new flat card.
When the headline's key word is a physical verb (split, merge, grow, cut), make the type perform that verb on itself in the first second, using a brand-coloured shape as the actor.
After a type pun has landed, resolve it (rejoin, settle) and push in on the resolved word, so the payoff is bigger than the setup.
When a sentence has a hero word and a connective tail, keep the tail at a quarter of the hero's size and use edge-of-frame texture to foreshadow the next beat's content.
When a number represents the burden the product removes, show it at its heaviest (edge-to-edge, alone) for a short beat, then transform it — never explain it.
When a total is being divided or shared, animate its tracking open so the characters separate, making division visible in the typography itself.
When showing what the product does to a number, keep the original number on screen and orbit the product's output around it, so cause and result read in one frame.
When two claims share a stem ('skip the ___'), keep the stem fixed and retype only the final word, so the change itself is the emphasis.
Before the densest frame of a film, insert a near-empty beat (one small mark on white) so the density lands by contrast.
When listing short adjectives, place them in a field of identical animated containers and make only the list items hold still, so stillness becomes the highlight.
When flashing several product features quickly, show them as cropped UI cards whose numbers are counting, so each card communicates one thing and the grid feels live.
When a claim ends on an abstract word (social, together, community), let literal images of that word arrive on top of it and then carry the cut to the next scene.
When the body of a film is maximal, end with a small logo on an empty field held for ~2s; the drop in energy does the emphasis.
When the product is a prompt box, open on the prompt box itself mid-move (tilted, blurred, glowing) and settle it into its device frame. Skip the establishing shot.
When the pain is indecision or a vague need, show it as a real user prompt being typed in the product's own input, in lowercase casual voice, instead of writing a marketing headline about it.
When a long user prompt contains 2-3 words that drive the output, zoom through the input field and re-type only those words huge, with the camera locked to the caret.
When an AI agent is 'thinking', replace the spinner with a tiny flat metaphor from the product's domain (ingredients into a pan, pages into a folder) plus a small status line.
When the AI returns a choice, show the candidates as a row and lift the chosen one out of line, on a full-bleed accent-colour flood timed to the music peak.
When a demo ends in a single action (order, send, deploy), push the camera into that one button and show a cursor press. Let the click be the climax, then leave the UI.
When the demo resolves the user's opening problem, cut to a small quiet sentence that restates the outcome in their language, in a void and at slow pace, as the counterweight to the busy demo.
When the resolution is two short lines, give both the identical reveal so they read as a couplet, and do not illustrate them literally.
When the film ends on quiet captions, set the lockup in the same face and size as those captions and hold it still for 2s or more.
When the hook is a problem statement, set it small in mono and colour only the painful verb in the pain colour; put the pain colour in an edge glow, not behind the text.
When the problem is 'too many X', show the X one at a time with fast swaps, then pull back to reveal them all stacked. The pull-back is the punchline.
When listing several pains, reuse one type treatment for all of them and change only the small UI-atom props around each one.
When a pain word is spatial ('buried', 'lost', 'hidden'), stage it literally with generic grey rows and one lit row, and move the heading up to give the metaphor the centre.
When the pain is money leaking, show a balance counter ticking down continuously (not a static number) with coins falling. End the problem act on it.
When the film pivots from problem to product, flip the whole palette on a hard cut with a short audio dip before it, and make the logo the first object in the new colour.
When the product detects or finds things, turn the logo into the hub of a radar sweep and let the problem's own objects blink in as targets.
When showing setup or onboarding, use one real modal on a slowly tilting glass plate with a cursor doing the 1-2 clicks, and quiet the music underneath.
When the payoff is a dense data table, tilt it in 3D with depth-of-field falloff and dolly across it. The viewer should feel its completeness, not read the cells.
When the message is 'how you get it' (extension, app store, CLI), isolate the one real install button in a void and press it.
When a dark film reaches its key benefit line, invert to a light field for that one line only, and swap words in place.
When a claim leads straight into an action, morph the claim word into a pill button in the same spot rather than cutting to a CTA card.
When the product flags one item, lift that row out of the table, give it the problem colour and dim the rest.
When stating parallel benefits ('No X / No Y'), hold the shared word still and swap only the variable word inside an accent pill.
When summarising before/after as identity, put a cutout person in front of one giant spaced word in the world's colour, with a tiny label phrase above.
When doing before/after, keep every layout variable identical and change only colour world plus one word; the viewer's eye does the comparison.
When the logo was already revealed at the turn, replay the identical reveal at the end and add only a tiny tagline, so the film rhymes.
When the opening VO line is 'verb + object + qualifiers', type only the verb-object large, then shrink the line to caption size as the qualifiers arrive.
When a VO sentence is too long for one card, break it at phrase boundaries and slide each phrase through the same centre line.
When the brand name first appears mid-sentence in the VO, set it inline at caption size with its icon as a glyph; save the big lockup for the end.
When the VO describes the input abstractly ('tell it about your X'), type a concrete example prompt on screen instead of captioning the VO.
When the product turns a long input into a single object, collapse the input container into a small named chip on an emptied background.
When the VO says the product fills something in automatically, show fields typing themselves with no cursor present.
When the VO says 'enable/turn on' features, show a grid of toggles flipping to the accent colour in stagger.
When walking through a setup flow, scroll one continuous panel instead of cutting between screens, so setup feels short.
At the 'launch/go live' beat, make the destination's icon lift out of the UI and zoom-through into the destination app; save the film's biggest 3D move for this beat.
When showing an AI scanning content, rack focus along a tilted feed so the sharp band acts as its attention.
When the VO says something is 'found', lift one item out of the crowded list onto an empty background.
When the demo reaches its outcome, return the background to the opening palette to signal resolution.
When the claim is 'a continuous stream', scroll many similar cards with the next one peeking in at half opacity.
When the film opened with a UI element emerging from the caption, end by collapsing the last UI element back into a chip in the closing caption.
When the opening line ends with the brand name, end the film on that same line and layout as the lockup.
When the opening line is about arrival or a new era, open with a decelerating radial motion that ends at the exact spot where the first word appears, and keep its residue (stars) as the background.
When a fintech/technical product wants to feel considered rather than hyped, set the opening line in a light condensed serif at ~5% H with per-word blur-in, and save sans for the UI.
When a sentence ends on the key verb, split it across two cards so the verb gets a card of its own.
When the copy says a verb of arrival (emerging, rising, here), make the product perform that verb in the very next beat.
When the name reveal and the product shot must share a beat, put the device inside the sentence as if it were a word, with the brand name on the same baseline.
When the product is conversational, morph the logo (or the name lockup) into the empty input field so the first demo begins from the brand.
When demoing an AI chat, type one specific, real-world question at human speed in an isolated input bar; specificity sells more than a generic prompt.
When the AI starts answering, change the light (bring the brand colour in) and stream the answer word by word, so the colour marks the AI's turn.
When a streamed AI answer cites a number, follow it immediately with the chart card, and use a moving highlight to point at the exact region the text described.
When a demo is split into chapters, give each chapter one word at 25-40% H over a full-frame colour flood, and keep the UI text tiny, so the scale jump itself signals a new chapter.
When a chat demo sets up a later payoff, bold the one clause (the trigger number) that the next scene will resolve.
When moving from a device to a data view, match the device's edge to the first line of the chart so the transition is a shape match, not a cut.
When a price or metric crosses a threshold the user set earlier, show only that line with the threshold gridline and mark the crossing with the single filled pill in the frame.
When the product acts on its own (alert, automation fires), show it as a native OS notification on a tilted device, with warmer light than the rest of the demo.
When repeating a chapter-title device, keep the type and move identical and change only the flood colour, spending the loudest colour on the action chapter.
When the product has a safety or judgement feature, show one exchange where it pushes back on the user; it does more for trust than any claim.
When the story needs the market or world to move, draw one line at full-frame size and let the background colour follow its direction (warm down, green up), with a real news notification as proof.
When the demo ends on a result number, punch into that UI pill until it is the largest UI text in the film, and keep it on screen for well under a second.
When a chapter is about thinking or review, use the coolest colour in the palette for its flood and let a small light element from the title carry into the next scene.
When the AI's long answer is itself the feature, stream it paragraph by paragraph and dim each finished paragraph so only one line is ever at full contrast.
When closing a long demo, burn to white through a flare and let the white contract into the small motif (a glint, a dot) that leads into the end card.
When you must credit a partner/infrastructure, set it as a small serif footnote riding a moving element toward the logo, not as its own card.
When the film's motif is light, have that light physically strike the logo on the loudest hit, then flatten the 3D mark into its 2D form.
When the opening used a signature light arc from one edge, close with the same arc from the opposite edge to bookend the film.
When VO and on-screen text say the same words, pop each word on its syllable with zero-frame cuts, and swap the brand name for the logo glyph inline.
When the VO adds an aside or afterthought, hand-write it small in a marker font next to the main line, like a margin note, instead of replacing the line.
When you need energy on a static line, flip the background colour on a beat while the text stays pinned in place; never move the text to create energy.
When the VO corrects itself ('wait, no'), cut to black and show only the interrupting word, swapped on the exact frame.
When the line says something is already achieved, put an empty checkbox before it and tick it as the word lands.
When the thesis line contains a deadline or number, underline only that with a hand-drawn stroke and keep everything else plain.
When the VO addresses the viewer in an aside, set it in parentheses in the accent colour, alone on a contrasting field.
When the VO lists products, hold the anchor word still and swap a quick line-drawing of each product next to it on the beat, rather than typing the names.
When a word means 'new' or 'breakthrough', surround it with hand-drawn burst ticks boiling on twos instead of a glow or scale pop.
When the VO rattles off a list of physical things, cut real macro footage every 10-15 frames under a single centred word that stays in the same position.
When one word names a process, animate that process inside the word's own letters and keep the rest of the line still.
When the line claims abundance ('enough', 'millions'), multiply a doodle until it fills the frame and use that fill as the transition.
When a sentence ends, let the accompanying doodle settle to rest on the full stop, so image and sentence finish together.
When the VO builds to a pivot word, step the size up word by word and set the pivot word in the accent typeface at about 2x.
When changing topic, build the wipe from a shape that belongs to the new topic (smoke for factories, water for oceans) rather than a generic wipe.
When the sentence is about making or assembling, drop the words in on scattered baselines and snap them into one line on the next beat.
When the VO lists many actors in a network, keep one role word centred and grow a swarm of hand-drawn arrows pointing at it.
When a number is coming, end the preceding line with a growing dash as a drumroll.
When a percentage is the payoff, show only the number big, with a hand-drawn burst, and give the unit its own separate beat.
When a sentence ends in a key term, set the lead-in small and quick, then cut to a new colour field just for the term.
When the VO stresses a small adverb (still, even, already), caret-insert it above the line in the marker voice instead of making it bold.
When the film turns to address the viewer, break the type scale once (the biggest word in the film) on the pivot word.
When the VO says something in a lowered voice or as an ironic aside, set it tiny in parentheses; scale can contradict the words for humour.
When a claim has a target year, flash the current year first and swap it to the target in the accent colour.
When the line says 'all of your X', surround the line with a crowd of real handwritten item names so each viewer can find theirs.
Reserve glow for the one line about light or power, so the effect means something.
When the line connects the viewer to the mission, draw an arrow from the 'you' word to the 'this' word.
When closing, repeat the film's opening device (here a self-correction) in a gentler form so the ending rhymes with the start.
End on the opening line set identically, then the URL with the key token in the accent voice.
When launching a feature inside an existing product, open mid-use on real UI (a live conversation, a filled form) and let the camera drift toward where the feature lives.
When a feature is a single button, push in until that button's label is headline-sized and show one cursor press. The UI label is the title.
When a click triggers the feature, cut on the click to a small quiet headline on white that names the feature, words rising in one by one, with a ~2% slow scale drift during the hold.
When the product has a mascot or avatar, give it one tiny idle animation (a blink) during the demo, just enough to make it a character.
When an action changes an object's audience (publish, share, export), morph the object out of its app context into a standalone card on a plain field.
When showing the recipient's side of a share flow, punch-in cut to their CTA button and click it.
When a share flow completes, end on the item arriving at the top of the recipient's list in a selected state, and push in slowly.
When the logo has an icon and a wordmark, show the icon alone first, then slide the wordmark out from behind it.
When the film is a studio/craft piece, open on a single small object framed by 1px guide lines that follow its bounds.
When revealing a set of screens, unfold them from behind a single card instead of fading them in separately.
When the goal is to show motion craft, move a set through two or three clean geometric formations, one eased move at a time.
To leave a scene of moving objects, accelerate them toward centre with motion blur and cut at peak speed to an inverted background.
When cutting from abstract shapes to real content, bring the content in with a blur-to-sharp scale-up as if the camera is focusing on it.
Before the reveal, hold a single breathing object that implies 'something is coming' (a typing indicator, a loading pulse) for 3–4 s.
When a 'something is coming' object precedes the logo, collapse it to a point and reveal the wordmark at that exact point.
When the news is 'our product now works inside X', open with the unfinished phrase 'Brand in…' and put the one glow on the preposition so the viewer waits for the partner name.
When listing integrations or partners, lock the sentence stem in place and swap only the partner logo inline at cap height, ~0.7s each.
When the music drops on a turn line, flash its first word or two across the frame at 40%+ H with motion blur, then cut to the full sentence at readable size.
When a claim has a statistic behind it, set the claim at readable size and put the source as a tiny footer line, not a second headline.
When the setup takes a real click path, show only the single decisive control, isolated and centred, and morph from its icon into its labelled state instead of showing the menu.
When a modal or form is the focus, invert the background behind it so the form is the only light surface in the frame.
When a demo's key action is a click, punch in ~3x on the button just before the click instead of adding a highlight ring.
When a prompt asks for 'N of something', pay it off with a grid that starts as placeholders, fills with real results, and then zooms out with acceleration until it overflows the frame.
After a maximal visual peak, name it in a small single line on a blank field while the music dips.
When the key word is about growth or scale, cut from the small line straight to a 4x crop of that word; the size jump performs the meaning.
When the launch is a feature with its own URL path, end on the URL alone at text size, with 'available now' as a tiny kicker, instead of a logo card.
When text tracks a VO word-for-word, → enter each new word in the brand accent and settle it to neutral when the next word lands, so colour marks 'now' without adding a second style.
When the sentence turns from subject to predicament, → enlarge the predicate word 1.5–2x and scroll the line so the new word lands at frame centre, dropping earlier words off-edge.
When one word names the problem in a bright film, → hard-cut to an inverted field for that single word and damage its letterforms, then cut straight back; use the inversion only once.
When listing items that share one source, → build each new item from the previous item's letters/container instead of cutting to a fresh layout.
When the VO ends on a verb of fixing (align, sort, sync, connect), → drop the verb from screen and animate the words themselves being fixed (dragged into order/size) on that syllable.
When the product is named mid-film, → cut to the first full-bleed brand-colour field of the film and show only icon+wordmark, leaving the claim sentence to VO.
When a feature is a single action with many outputs, → put the action as one centred pill and float its real outputs around it at smaller scale, never a grid.
When moving from 'the feature' to 'using the feature', → morph the feature's label/button into its input field and type a realistic prompt there, rather than cutting to a screenshot.
When an action triggers the payoff, → punch in to the button for ~1s, click, and morph the button into the first element of the result.
When the claim is automation, → show the same system output row repeating on a machine rhythm (fixed interval, auto-scroll), using the audience's native UI idiom.
When a list should feel endless, → move it onto a tilted 3D surface where individual rows are unreadable and keep it scrolling as the camera drifts away.
When leaving a busy demo for the summary claims, → return to the film's opening type system at small size on empty white so the closing reads as a bookend.
When VO lists parallel adjectives after one stem, → keep the stem fixed and swap only the adjective in the same slot, accent-coloured.
When the last item of a parallel list changes grammar or scope, → break the fixed-stem pattern and give it its own centred line and a longer hold.
When the VO ends on a slogan, → put the URL and 1–2 action buttons on screen instead of the slogan, with the primary action in the accent colour, and hold still 3–4s.
When the hook needs context before the first line, drift a few depth-blurred UI windows and introduce one accent-coloured object that will lead the eye into the text.
When the hook is a question to the viewer, pair it with a small object that implies the answer action (a send icon, a compose window) rather than a big type treatment.
When the 'product' is a service or craft, show a stylised brand-coloured version of the tool used (timeline, canvas) instead of a real screenshot.
When listing 3 services in a fast promo, give each its own beat as a single labelled pill centred on screen, on the music hits.
When a list is shown as identical repeated beats, invert the background on the middle or most important item to break the pattern.
In a light-stage film, cut to black only once, for the mid-film brand reveal, and hit it with a radial light burst on a music accent.
When showing portfolio work, present one piece at a time in a centred carousel with arrow controls, not a crowded grid.
When the CTA is a booking, colour the low-commitment word (discovery, free, quick) rather than the action noun.
When the CTA is a booking or signup, act out the full flow in two or three clicks right after stating it.
When closing, echo an earlier line's structure and accent word so the ending feels like a callback.
When the logo has a strong counter or shape, bring it in oversized so its hole frames the previous line, then spin and shrink it to size as the transition; save the film's only overshoot for this.
When locking up, reveal mark, name and tagline in that order, one after another, and hold at least 2-3s.
If you use a special type fill (chrome, gradient), spend it once on the very first word and let it resolve to the plain type colour.
When the opening phrase is two to three words, give each word its own card and link them with a horizontal whip so they read as one phrase.
When the line is emotional ('ready', 'finally'), cut to the film's first atmospheric photo and blur the type in instead of wiping it.
At the turn from situation to action, cut from a dark to a light world and have the new words land in the brand hue before settling to ink.
When the tagline ends in an action verb, render that verb as a button, click it, and zoom through the button into the next scene.
When showing a portfolio of different products, keep one device and set fixed and cut only the screen content, accelerating the swaps at the end.
When showing a client-logo wall, make every logo one grey tone and scatter them around a centred headline.
One beat before a big metaphor shot, plant a subtle hint of it (orbit lines before a rocket) in the background.
When the brand verb appears in a sentence, mark it quietly (capital or hue) one beat before giving it a full-screen moment.
If you must use a literal metaphor (rocket for launch), lock the word in place and cut the footage underneath at ~0.4 s for about a second only.
When the domain contains the film's key word, drop that word to small size and type the rest of the URL onto it.
If the name or URL was just shown, the end card can be the bare mark on an empty frame, slowly receding.
When a hook is split setup/payoff across two cuts, make the payoff line about twice the setup's size and land it on the first music hit.
When 'introducing' follows a line about chance or uncertainty, decode it from random digits like a slot reel so the resolve reads as certainty.
After a chaotic decode, hold the resolved word for about a second with a slow push and a light sweep before the name appears.
When the name follows a scramble, fill its letters in out of order (not left to right) so the name reveal rhymes with the decode.
When a claim is about the product's core experience, lay oversized type over the live UI so the UI becomes the claim's backdrop rather than its illustration.
When a line over UI carries the brand's key word, defocus the UI behind it and colour only that word so it can be called back later.
When stacking several claims over UI, swap to the UI screen that proves each claim rather than keeping one generic screen.
When setting up a headline number, flip the world's polarity and keep the lead-in tiny, with one word in a contrasting italic serif.
When revealing a headline money figure, count it up quickly in a dedicated display face used nowhere else, alone on a light field, and hold ~1s at the final value.
When a count is too large to show ('175+ pairs'), put a few recognisable icons on a continuously rotating arc so more keep arriving, in the bottom third under the text.
When a film has a light 'reward' act, put partner/trust credits in the same light world and accent face so trust and reward read as one register.
When the closing slogan repeats a word from an earlier claim, give it the identical colour treatment so the callback is recognised instantly.
When wiping to the end card, use a giant fragment of the logo mark as the wipe shape, then assemble the mark at normal size.
When a film uses light leaks and glitch throughout, strip them all from the end card and let the mark be the only colour on flat black.

When the audience is designers and the product is a canvas tool, open on a macro of the user's artwork and draw the tool's own guides (grid, handles) over it before revealing the UI, so the hook is craft, not chrome.
When establishing where a feature lives, pull back continuously from the content to the full app in one move instead of cutting to a wide screenshot.
When a feature is invoked by a small icon, punch in so the icon appears within a cursor-length of where the eye already is, then click it.
When the product is prompt-driven, type the user's request live in the real input (1 char/frame) and land the send click on a music accent.
When an action will produce many outputs, pull the camera back before they appear so the frame has empty space waiting for them.

When a section title overlays a live demo, set it small in a top-left corner and reveal per word in the brand's selection colour, settling to neutral as the next word lands, so type never competes with the UI for the centre.
When a per-word title must leave quickly, play its entrance in reverse (re-highlight then remove each word) rather than fading the whole line.
When the claim is abundance or breadth ('explore wide', 'hundreds of options'), cut a stepped zoom-out burst of 6–8 cuts, 2 frames apart, rather than one smooth pull-back.
When you show a wall of generated outputs, hold the camera and let a named cursor pick one, so abundance resolves into a human decision.
When a choice is made from many options, push in on the chosen one in 2–3 stepped cuts, keeping the chooser's cursor in frame.
When selling an AI tool to craftspeople, insert a short beat of manual tweaking between AI actions to show the human stays in control.
When a script pairs opposites (wide/deep, fast/careful), flip the frame's density with them: crowded grid for one, near-empty panel for the other.
When a demo's prompt carries the message, write it as the user's goal in their words and type it live rather than captioning it.
When showing an AI reasoning step, hold ~2s on the product's real thinking indicator with nothing else moving.
When the film has a signature text-reveal, reuse it for the product's own streamed output so 'newly generated' has one consistent visual meaning.
When the product generates UI, show the empty container for ~6 frames before its contents fill in.
When showing several design alternatives, give 2–3 of them a 1s full-bleed macro each before pulling back to the grid.
When the UI element represents a value (progress, count, level), animate it filling to its value during the showcase shot.
When a film has two demo chapters, repeat the same choose-with-a-teammate beat in both so the structure rhymes.
When a chosen option must be committed, show it physically dragged into its final place with a slight in-flight tilt, not swapped by a cut.
When a film has chapters, use one identical title treatment and position for every chapter header so the structure is learned by the second one.
When an abstract capability maps to a single control, show the control being switched instead of illustrating the concept.
When revealing a generated sequence of screens, place the existing screen first and stagger the new ones in reading order.
When the change is too small to see (spacing, alignment, 1px), cut to an extreme macro and show the tool's own measurement readout counting to the new value.
After a macro of one change, pull back to show the same marker repeated across all instances.
When the audience is expert, show tool-native markers (component frames, tokens, handles) as proof of real output instead of labelling it.
When a list is generated, go macro and stagger each item in as a shimmer skeleton that resolves, ~4 frames apart.
When one command changes many items at once, stagger the change across them in reading order so it reads as propagation.
When a demo transforms something, end on the same framing you opened on so before/after is implicit.
When revealing the product name, cut to the film's only black frame and dress the line in one gesture from the product's UI (selection box, cursor) rather than a generic effect.
When the brand mark is made of simple shapes and the product is a design tool, assemble the logo from separate selected shapes on black.
When closing, hold the logo small on black for 1.3s+ with the music already faded out.
When the film opens on a question for a technical audience, open on an empty caret for a few frames before the first glyph.
When the subject is AI or code, reveal the hook word by scramble-decode with a light source on the caret, starting at display size.
When a question ends on its key noun, type the setup, shrink it away, and give the key noun its own frame.
When isolating the key noun of a question, change one type property only for it (tracking, weight or case) and hold it longest while slowly receding.
When a question scene hands over to its answer, invert the background on a hard cut but carry the framing motif (brackets) across.

When the whole story happens inside one surface (a lock screen, an inbox), open with a sub-second wide of the device on a neutral field, then cut in; the wide tells the viewer where they are so the macro needs no context.
When the problem can be shown as one real message a user receives, cut to it in macro and let the UI copy state the problem; do not write a headline for it.
When the product's value is 'it answers before you ask', show the question first and have the product's native UI element arrive on top of it, with one small sound on the arrival.
When a story began on a wide, return to the exact same wide after the macro, with a decelerating pull and a small settle, so the viewer understands the loop is closed.

When the news is a platform/availability announcement, type the sentence per word in plain small text and put the only colour on the platform word (its icon peeking from behind it) at the end of the line.
When the lockup is mark + name, show the mark alone first at 2–3x its final size, then shrink it to cap height so the name can arrive next to it.
When text has been typed per word earlier in the film, build the end lockup with the same per-word reveal so the end card feels like part of the same film.
When a tagline is typed on an empty field, start at 2-3x final size and pull back as it grows, and type the payoff word in the single accent colour.
When one word of a finished line must become the next scene's trigger, erase the other words (blur-out from the left) rather than enlarging the key word.
When the tagline contains a verb of transformation, make a cursor click on the key word be the transition, blooming the new world from the click point.
When the product UI appears for the first time, fly it in on a 3D tilt that settles over 45-60 frames, cropped close first and pulled back second.
When demoing a multi-step filter, push in on the single control column and let each click change exactly one thing, with ~1-1.5s between clicks.
When a UI action produces a result list worth showing off, lift the result items out of the app window onto an empty field and stagger them in.
When opening a detail view, lift the clicked row out and grow it into the detail card, instead of cutting to a new screen.
When the feature is a one-click action, push until the button fills the frame and keep its unclicked siblings visible as the 'before'.
When ending a demo chapter, pull back to the whole product floating small before the next chapter card.
When a demo film has chapters, reuse the opening title treatment verbatim for each chapter card and colour only the feature noun.
When a line is about people, surround the text with depth-blurred avatar circles at the frame edges, never overlapping the words.
When a claim is followed by the UI that fulfils it, reuse the claim's decorative elements (avatars) as the objects that fly into the UI.
When a film uses a recurring graphic device (caret, bar, dot), build the logo reveal out of that device.
When locking up icon + wordmark, reveal the icon alone first, then slide it aside and write the wordmark, holding the finished lockup for about 2s.
When opening on the problem, set the topic line small and let a single warning-coloured light source own the frame; save large type for the payoff.
When the pain is time, show time passing (a scrubbing timeline or ticking calendar) under the line rather than just stating the duration.
When stating a cost, put a gauge or meter under it pinned toward the maximum, so magnitude reads through the instrument while type stays small.

When pivoting from problem to solution, change the entire world colour on a single moving object (needle, sweep, wipe), and let it flicker between the two states once or twice before the new one wins.
When a dark film reaches 'Introducing', spend its single brightest/whitest frame and its one glitch there, and nowhere else.
When the product is a sub-brand, render the parent name neutral and the new product word in the solution colour.
When a claim has a symbolic object as its noun, put the object centre and split the rest of the sentence into opposite corners so the eye reads across the object.
When a feature claim names an environment, follow it with the real third-party logos in a UI card rather than illustrating it.
When a solution number answers an earlier problem number, keep every line before it at caption size so the answer is the first large type in the act.
When introducing a jargon acronym, spread its letters apart as nodes in a small diagram so it reads slowly and suggests how it is built.
When a solution act can echo a problem-act instrument (gauge, timeline), bring it back in the solution colour showing the good value.
When a sentence's verb is something the product does in one click, replace the word inline with the UI control and animate it from off to on.
When a film has a feature act and a closing act, insert a <1s logo-mark stamp between them as a chapter divider.
When the payoff line contains the problem's name, show that name huge and bleeding off-frame first, then pull back so it shrinks to sit beside the benefit word.
When a contrast line negates the opening pain ('not months'), isolate 'not' for a beat and make the negated callback the largest type, not the positive half.
After the biggest type of the closing act, drop the next line back to caption size and dim the lighting to create a runway into the end card.
When the end card has a CTA button, show a cursor clicking it once so the action is modelled, not just offered.
When a hook is a setup for a contrast, keep the setup line object-free and colour only the phrase that the next line will replace.
When a contrast pair is shown, swap the second line into the exact slot of the first and give only the winning line a literal object that performs its verb.
When a sentence names a concrete thing the company makes, place a small icon of it inline between the words instead of below or beside the line.
When a clicked element leads to more detail, let the detail card emerge from the clicked element in place rather than cutting to it.
Alternate object beats with empty text-only beats, so each object beat arrives against a clean field.
When a dense montage must coexist with text, arrange the imagery as a ring around the frame edge and keep a clean empty centre for the line.
When leaving a crowded frame, scatter everything outward and keep one element as the survivor that carries into the next beat.
When a claim is about readiness or process, morph the previous object into a progress bar whose stage labels foreshadow the film's closing line.
When showing portfolio proof, reveal a grid then have a cursor pick one item that lifts while the rest defocus.
When a claim is about spread or reach, put the content on an orbit path around the line so it circulates without covering it.
When you have strong metrics, keep the headline qualitative and put the numbers small in a realistic table underneath as evidence.
When the CTA follows proof, collapse the proof to its best item and attach the CTA button to that item, then click it.
In a film built on a pale neutral field, withhold the full-frame brand colour for a single ~1s beat just before the closing summary.
When closing on a list of services, build it cumulatively one word per beat and put the differentiator last, on its own line, in the accent colour.
When the film's voice is restrained, keep the lockup at body-text scale and hold it still for 3-4s rather than making it the loudest frame.
When VO says 'Introducing <feature>', put only the feature noun on screen, small and alone in a void, and let it land 0.1-0.2s before the word is spoken.
When the VO names the brand right after the feature, morph the feature word into the brand mark (use the mark's own geometry as the eraser) instead of cutting to a logo card.
When VO describes an input→output process, show the inputs (real thumbnails) physically travelling into the real UI control, and do not caption the sentence.

When the product creates something intangible (a voice, a style, a model), give it one abstract hero object (orb/sphere), bloom it on the music swell, and reuse that same object later as avatar and background.
After an abstract 'creation' visual, land on a concrete named artifact with realistic copy (name + one-line descriptor) and hold it ~2s.
When VO claims 'one X powers many Y', draw a single node forking into 2-3 branches that resolve into real Y items; glow only while they are generating.
When VO poses a rhetorical 'prefer X?' question, don't show the question; empty the frame for a breath and answer with the single UI control that does X.
When showing a recording/capture step, expand the trigger button into the panel and use red (only here) for the live playhead and waveform.
When the VO pays off an earlier setup ('your own voice'), bring back the earlier metaphor object at full-frame scale on the music swell and hold it longer than any other beat.
When VO says 'or just pick from X', show the real app nav and step the selection highlight to X in 3-4 quick hops, which also previews sibling features.
When VO claims breadth ('library', 'hundreds of'), show one dense real grid page at mid-scale for ~2s without zooming into any item, then recede it on a breath.
When a launch covers 2+ features, give every feature title the identical treatment (same size, position, reveal) so the repetition itself says 'new chapter'.
When the concept is 'consistency across many items', arrange the items in an orbit around one centre, and hold back saturated colour until this beat so it lands as new.
When a tech film needs its emotional peak, cut to real warm human photography (grain, flash) in a fast 3-panel montage at ~75-85% of runtime, with no text on top.
When exiting a high-energy montage into the end card, wipe with a giant version of the logo's shape and scale it down into the centred mark.
When the opening used a logo morph, end with its reverse (close → open) so the film is visibly bookended.
When the VO closes on a tagline, keep the tagline off screen: show only wordmark + typed URL and hold still 3-5s while the music fades.
When the stage is black, light it with one large brand-coloured glow from a frame edge and keep all objects in the dark half.
When the brand is well known and the film is about a flow, flash the wordmark out of the icon and retract it, keeping the icon as the object that will transform.
When moving from logo to product UI, morph the logo shape into the UI's primary element and reveal its label only after the shape has settled.
When a list of UI rows appears, have each row slide out from under the previous one with a 4-6 frame stagger so the list grows as one object.
When clearing a staggered stack, collapse it in reverse order at a faster stagger than it entered.
When morphing a UI element into the next screen, interpolate its fill from the current colour to the dominant colour of the destination content.
When a flow film ends on the product's core screen, hold that screen as the ending rather than cutting to a logo.
When the hook quotes a promise the film will refute, show it as clean product-style UI and deface it with a hand-drawn mark within half a second, so the mark itself is the 'but'.
When the script pivots with 'but', invert background luminance on a hard cut but keep the repeated word at the same screen position so the eye doesn't have to re-find the line.
When word-by-word kinetic type forces a filler word onto its own beat, let a background diagram do the moving and leave the word itself plain.
When the camera tracks along a sentence, draw a hand-marker arrow from the previous word to the next one so the eye leads the camera instead of chasing it.
When a second accent colour is needed, bind it to one meaning (error/wrong) and introduce it on the first word that carries that meaning.
After 4-5 rapid single-word beats that each drew a mark, pull back once to show all the marks together as a small diagram and hold it; the viewer gets the sum before the punchline.
When a line has one key term, set the line with a visible gap for it, fill the gap last, then punch in to ~3x on that term.
When the script says something is outdated or stuck in the past, pan against reading direction along a dated timeline and overshoot to an absurdly old year.
When moving between two diagram scenes, reuse the lines of the first as the structure of the second (axis → grid) instead of cutting.
When describing a manual chore, show a cursor physically typing one value into one highlighted cell of an otherwise empty tool; one small concrete action beats a full busy screen.
When the words name a physical action ('by hand'), make the cursor that body part and let it do the action slightly clumsily, knocking one element off the grid.
When the problem peaks, let the error colour you seeded earlier multiply until it fills the object, using a real failure detail from the tool (e.g. '###') rather than a generic warning icon.
When turning from problem to solution, collapse the problem visual into one small unit, recolour it to the brand accent, hold it still for ~0.4s, then grow it (stepped) into the next scene.
When revealing a short product name, shrink 'Introducing' to caption size against the name's baseline and assemble the name's glyphs in a stagger rather than fading it in as a block.
When closing a film built on a hand-drawn mark language, replay those marks around the logo and erase them to leave it clean, but then hold the clean logo for at least 1.5s.
When a launch is 'a new section in an existing product', open cropped tight on the navigation where the new entry will appear, not on the whole app.
When you need the viewer to notice something NEW in a UI, first walk the cursor across 1–2 existing items so the new one reads as an addition to a known row.
When the feature is a new menu/tab/section, reveal its NAME by typing it into the real nav while neighbours slide apart, before any title card says it.
When a click will trigger the next scene, hold ~1s on the target before the click so the name is read, then let the click motivate the camera move.
When going from a control to the screen it opens, pull back continuously from the control instead of cutting, so the cause stays on screen.
When the feature is a collection/library, show it filling item by item on a staggered load rather than cutting to the finished grid.
When switching from demo to title card, hard-cut to a darker shade of the same hue and spend the one contrasting accent on a tiny kicker label, not on the title.
When the product name is a two-part 'brand + feature' title, set it large, bottom-left, and pop the two words ~7 frames apart so the feature word lands as the second hit.
When adding availability/status under a title, use a tiny mono line typed in after the title has landed, never the same face and never simultaneously.
When the whole film uses typing as its reveal, build the end logo the same way: icon alone, then the wordmark typed out as the icon slides aside.
When holding an end logo for 3s+, keep the logo still and let only a small brand-specific texture animate at the edges.
When a film opens with direct address ('Are you', 'You'), set those words giant and let them bleed off the edge while tracking, synced to the VO.
When a single adverb carries the emotion of the question ('still', 'again', 'yet'), give it its own card.
After a giant-word hook, drop the rest of the sentence to body size so the hook's scale stays special.
When the VO names a tedious category ('job boards', 'tools', 'apps'), scroll many real instances through a selection frame at slot-machine speed instead of typing the category word.
When the problem is a human routine, place the words behind a cut-out person (occluded by the head) so the text reads as their situation; dress or light them in the brand colour.
When the VO lists chores in parallel, keep one shot and swap the caption while adding clutter, so the chores accumulate.
At the turn from clutter to solution, zoom into one element of the clutter until it fills the frame and reveal the product name inside it.
When a benefit sentence follows the name, reuse the name's framing device to carry the words, and isolate the audience word ('you') to echo the hook.
When the benefit is a single user action, show only the verb, huge, inside a button shape.
When the VO promises that others come to the user, show the arrival state (a welcome message, an invite) instead of a search screen.
When the script calls back to the opening pain as a command ('stop X'), frame the line with fixed guide lines/crosshairs so it reads as settled.
At the release after a problem-heavy film, cut to the first open, expansive image, and render it in the film's texture so it doesn't feel like stock.
When a title writes on per letter, lead the write head with a soft light or colour orb so the reveal has a visible cause, and let the light exit once the word is complete.
When a micro-promo has a single-adjective claim, cut hard to a full-frame brand-colour slab for exactly one beat and change the type weight from the title's.
After loud full-frame type beats, introduce the UI small in empty space and push in, so the scale drop pulls the viewer closer.
When showing a prompt being typed, crop so tight the field bleeds off-frame and track the caret with the camera, rather than showing the whole input.
When a demo reaches its key click, reframe to only the target control and shift the background tint to mark the hand-off.
When listing benefits in a product demo, present them as the product's output with per-item progress rings that complete one by one.
When a loopable film opens on a big title, end on the same words tiny with a full stop, so the loop point is a scale jump.
When the hook is a rhetorical question, open on its most loaded word alone at 35–45% frame height within the first 3 frames.
When the problem is a repetitive chore, let an accent stroke keep looping around the caption instead of settling.
Before a punchline card, whip the brand gradient across an empty frame for 3–4 frames instead of cutting straight to it.
When a setup phrase leads into a punchline, bring it in on the momentum of the previous transition and dim it before the punchline lands.
When the punchline of the hook is a single number or date, slam it in from 4–5x with motion blur, then let it creep smaller during the hold.
At the turn ('Meet', 'Introducing'), reuse the hook word's exact type treatment so the two read as a pair.
Save the first solid fill of the accent colour for the product name; before that, use the accent only as light or stroke.
When a claim is about serving people, orbit small, desaturated photo tiles around the caption so the text stays the hero.
When showing KPIs, use at most two cards, count up with an ease-out and hold the final value for at least 1 s.
When the claim is 'many sources, one place', gather many varied cards into a single continuous arc under the headline.
When a demo prompt is long, start typing it large and scale it down as it grows, so the first words are read and the rest is only seen.
When the demo ends on a submit click, morph the button into an iris that opens onto the end card.
When a stroke motif ran through the film, reveal the end wordmark as that stroke drawing on and then filling.
End the film on the first fully still frame: wordmark, tiny tagline, one CTA pill, held for about 3 s.
When opening a type-only piece on a dark stage, shrink a small glowing object to a point at the exact spot the first word will appear.
When a product name is a short phrase, show it one word per beat, each settling from oversized dark grey to white, and tint only the final noun.
When a type showcase switches from demo words to a claim, hard-cut the stage polarity (dark → white) and put one slowly rotating object behind the line.
When a film is a series of text beats, use one recurring tiny motif at centre as the section divider.
When a line is a parallel couplet, build both lines from shared word objects that slide between rows, and use a travelling accent tint to guide reading order.
When a sentence is a setup whose payoff comes in the next beat, keep it at caption size and exit it word by word so the payoff arrives on an empty stage.
When the payoff word is about premium or value, reveal it with a wide-tracking-to-tight collapse, since open tracking reads as luxury.
When a long type-only piece needs structure, alternate dark 'showing' sections with short white 'claim' interludes at a regular interval.
When listing 2-4 short words on one line, tint each word in the accent while it animates and let it cool to neutral once settled, so the colour marks reading order.
When a sentence says what matters, set it small and then remove every word except the one that matters, instead of enlarging it.
When closing a type-only film, repeat the exact opening word-by-word device with the product category words, so the structure rhymes.
When a headline is 'Noun, qualifier', set the noun Bold and the qualifier Light in the same size, so weight carries the hierarchy without resizing.
When the film opens with a quiet headline, turn it into a pressable pill and start the music on the press, so the viewer's attention and the energy change happen on the same frame.
When the next line is about flow or motion, let a ribbon or line sweep through as the transition and leave it running under the new text.
When two parallel claims are stacked, set the second in the heavier weight; parallel lines read as a set, and the weight tells you which one to keep.
When you need a palette-cleanser mid-film, invert to a light 'blueprint' scene and show an element being constructed on the grid before the text appears in it.
When a line is 'Problem— Answer', type it with a caret under a music dip and set the problem grey-regular and the answer white-bold.
When moving from the last text line to the logo, squash the line into a thin horizon and rise the mark out of it, instead of a crossfade.
When the next shot is a hero object rising from below, place the glow under the title first so the light already marks where the object will enter.
When handing focus from title to product, raise the product through the title (occluding its centre letters) and fade the title behind it instead of cutting.
When listing 2-3 small features of one product, float them as tiny glass pills around the hero in a triangle, and animate only one of them (a counter).
When a title claims breadth ('tools', 'templates'), follow it with an evenly spaced row of real screens cropped at both frame edges, implying the set continues.
When moving from many to one, whip the group out of frame and land a single hero on a lit pedestal, with the headline moved to the top so the object owns the centre.
When a shot needs to feel 'premium' and still, use an isometric field of identical objects with exactly one lit, but cap the hold around 3s unless something changes.
When a claim is abstract ('scale', 'without limits'), print it on the product's own screen and put the device in a tactile material setting instead of overlaying type.
When closing the product section before the end card, iris the scene down to a single dot and let that dot become the anchor of the closing line.
When the CTA is a question, type the statement first and add the '?' as its own late beat.
When the product is an agent/bot, open on a tiny mascot doing one human micro-action (eyes opening) in an otherwise empty frame.
When the news is a new capability, show the character acquiring the object first and hold back the caption until the viewer has guessed it.
When you need the viewer to look at an object, make the character look at it; eye direction beats arrows.
When the claim is surprising on its own, state it deadpan: small type, appearing whole, held long, with the character reacting to camera.
When the mascot is also the logo, clear the frame, turn it into its icon pose, and shrink it to icon size before the wordmark appears.
When a mascot carried the film, the lockup should be the mascot shrunk to icon size with the wordmark typed beside it; no new graphics.
When the product is framed as a person or colleague, open on the giant word 'Meet' alone on the first hit, and delay the noun to the next card.

When a product fills many roles, lock the stem 'Your new AI' and cascade the roles vertically in a slot-machine list, ordered from smallest to most ambitious, with one colour accent chasing the active item.
When a script alternates action verbs and connecting words, make only the verbs giant (35-45% H, bleeding off the frame) and set the connective phrases small.
When the copy's verb maps to a UI control (send, build, generate), zoom through a giant version of that control's icon and come out on the real button.
When showing a generative product's prompt, write it oddly specific (a niche, named details) so the result feels real and not canned.
When showing a generated result, float the real UI on a tilted 3D plane with depth of field and let a background light bloom as it completes.
When revealing the product's category term, split the lead-in phrase and the term across two cards and give the term the only colour/gradient on type in the film, after a music dip.
When showing a roster of agents or options, tilt the list in 3D and have one oversized cursor tap one item, rather than showing all of them equally.
When the product is 'AI employees', prove it with named agents leaving role-specific comments on real output.
When listing three verbs, give each its own giant card on the beat and make the core verb the one solid, fully sharp word.
When the benefit is about autonomy or not needing you, set it small on an emptied frame right after the loudest type, so the stillness says it.
When the demo used a distinctive cursor, reuse it at giant scale as the wipe into the end card.
When the film is loud and optical, end on the opposite: a light serif wordmark on a flat brand colour with zero motion for ~3s.
When the hook is a short imperative that the product responds to, type it at a scale too big for the frame and track the caret, so the viewer experiences the input before seeing the whole sentence.
When a giant caret-follow line finishes, pull back in ≤6 frames to show the whole sentence small and hold ~0.5s. The reading happens on the small version, not during the big type.
When a list's first item is the headline and the rest are qualifiers, give the first item its own frame in the accent colour, then shrink it into the full line.
When a list item is added to a line that is already on screen, scale the whole line down as it types instead of reflowing or cutting, so the eye stays on one centred block.
When the script pivots to 'Meet / Introducing', show that one word alone at large size and use the brand's ambient light (glow or gradient) as a curtain that floods and retracts before the name.
When revealing a logo whose mark is a simple geometric glyph, give the mark a single outward burst of its own geometry and settle it to size; add the wordmark only after the mark is still.
When moving from abstract brand frames to the product demo, change the background to a soft-focus photograph with a tonal palette so the UI card is the only sharp, high-contrast object.
When showing a 'send/submit' click, visualise it with the film's own ambient light passing through the component (≈10 frames) rather than a stock ripple, then move the component to its next role.
When an AI step has a wait or status state, crop in on the single status line and hold it briefly, so its resolution (checkmark) lands in the same place the eye is already looking.
When revealing an AI-generated result, pull back from the request so that request and output sit side by side in one frame, instead of cutting to the output alone.

When the demo ends on a commit action (publish, send, merge), punch in until the button dominates the frame and change its state to the brand accent. Keep the accent reserved for 'go' actions across the whole film.
When a film has shown its proof, bring back the opening line with inverted polarity (dark↔light) and emphasise only the key verb, so the repeat reads as a payoff and not filler.
When the claim is breadth ('any X'), show many small, varied outputs drifting at different depths on a flat brand-colour field for 2–3s, too many to read one by one.
When a word names a coding or AI process step, reveal it with a scramble-decode that resolves L→R over ~12 frames, stepping on twos, and give each step in the list its own colour.
When a list is a sequence of process steps, carry each step to the next with the same ambient-light flood and end the sequence on the brand colour.
When a feature is 'works with any X', show the X logos in a slowly rotating ring around a small label for under 1s; a grid would read as a spec sheet.
When a metric qualifies a claim, first show the claim without it, then part the words and grow a count-up into the gap with an ease-out on the value (big steps early, +1 at the end).
When the claim concerns code or developer workflow, frame the sentence in a code glyph ({ }, </>, $) that opens first to make room, then type the words inside.
When the end-state of the product is one action, isolate that button on black, type its label, click it, and let its fill wipe L→R as a progress bar.
When restating the core instruction near the end, reuse the hook's typing device at a smaller scale and speed, so the film is bookended by the same gesture.
When locking up, return to the exact background world of the hook and repeat the mark-then-name order used at the first reveal.
When ending a high-energy film, set the CTA small (≈3% cap) on the same background as the lockup, reveal it word by word, and hold ≥2s with the url at half its size.
When the product's pitch is speed/ease, cold-open on the first real click (a verb-labelled button + cursor) instead of a title card.
When a click opens a dialog, grow the clicked element into the dialog (empty first, content staggered in ~0.3s later) instead of cutting.
When selecting one option in a UI demo, push to a macro crop and mark the choice with a single diagonal light sweep + check, and never glow the unselected options.
When a UI flow sets up a speed claim, end the flow on the confirm click and cut straight to the claim.
When a claim has a setup and a payoff ('Launch in / one day'), put the setup on its own screen small and brief, and exit it before the payoff arrives.
When a speed/time claim follows a demo, give the number phrase its own screen and a slow scale-up during the hold; make it the only text that grows.
When enumerating customisable items, run a rolling slot-list on one side and fill the matching real UI field on the other side in sync, one item per ~0.6s.
When moving from product demo to closing statement, flip the background luminance once with a feathered wipe and carry one element (the user's logo) across it.
When the closing claim arrives, set it as the largest type in the film on the inverted background and push in slowly until it crops.
When the punchline is 'your X' (white-label, personalisation), type it in with a caret and an input underline so it reads as a blank for the viewer to fill.
When the opening is a short phrase typed word by word, start the first word large and shrink the line as words arrive so it always fits.
When a phrase ends on the benefit word, track the camera to centre that word, mute the preceding words, and give only it the gradient fill.
When cutting after a push-in, start the next shot already scaling in the same direction so the zoom carries through the cut.
When type is larger than the line fits, track the camera with the newest word and let earlier words exit the opposite edge.
Before a stat reveal, strip the frame to small black type on empty white for about half a second, ending on a dangling connector word.
When a multiplier stat must feel big without big type, spawn concentric rings outward from its container while the number counts up.

title: Checklist ticks off, then the editor opens
why: Seeing named steps complete one at a time makes instant output feel like real effort, so the finished result earns trust instead of looking like magic.

title: Capability line morphs into a typed prompt
why: A text-only pause between demos restates the thesis, recasts what was just shown, and primes the viewer for how the next demo will work.

title: Switching on agent mode with a light-to-dark flip
why: The bright-to-dark inversion signals we are inside a real product and a special mode just engaged, shifting tone from plain utility to AI storytelling with no copy needed.

title: Study findings turn into re-created ad loops
why: A tighter second look at proof the viewer already believes adds credibility, shows the footage is genuinely playing, and masks the scene change, all without extra text.

title: Dragging in existing clips and naming the feature
why: Watching their own clips dragged into the tool tells the viewer it builds on assets they already have, rather than only producing new material.

title: A detailed brief is typed and answered
why: The second prompt goes from a bare link to full creative direction in the user's voice, showing the system follows instructions and not just setup input.

title: Closing offer ends on an agent sign-off
why: The offer reads like a sentence the viewer completes mentally; the word swap makes the ending feel earned, and two italic words flag what to remember.

title: Headline built word by word with credentials
why: Words assembling into a headline hold attention without any transition, and each landing is taken as a plain statement of fact rather than a flourish.

title: Stepping into the app to pick an order type
why: Establishing early that we are on an actual phone in a working app means later taps read as genuine use, not decoration.

title: Dialing in values and finishing the order form
why: A single gesture shifts four figures together, letting the viewer grasp how the control drives the money outcome with no narration.

title: Placing the order and receiving confirmation
why: The fastest, most tactile moment in the piece turns a flat closing prompt into a journey, making the brand feel crafted rather than templated.

title: Files sort themselves, then pass to the next scene
why: Each new row appears as the folders reshuffle, so scattered personal material seems already filed, and the viewer accepts the structure without having it explained.

title: Question morphs into the product's answer
why: With the split question and clutter in the middle, viewers answer for themselves before any name appears; the card flipping off turns that answer into the reveal's lead-in.

title: Live widgets settle into the closing line
why: Four convincing data panels appear in under four seconds, each animating a figure or shape on entry, so the product feels operational rather than a set of screenshots.

title: Typing a request, sending it, leaving the scene
why: Seeing a real sentence typed into a familiar message box turns an abstract tool into me asking it something, in my own words.

title: Closing claim collapses into icon and wordmark
why: The ingredient list is read in single-word steps, then folds into the benefit line, so the closing claim feels earned by the first instead of asserted.

title: Headline, generated image, and audience reaction
why: Word-by-word reading lets viewers finish the sentence themselves, while a highlight box singles out the claim word, so the whole promise registers before any product appears.

title: Composing a prompt and pressing send
why: One unbroken motion shows the work product becoming input and the request being typed, so the interface explains itself with no voiceover or labels.

title: Generated variations settle into the brand ending
why: One request yields many options, and fanning them out hands the eye a choice, communicating abundance in just over a second.

title: A single click cascades before emphasis lands
why: One admin action ripples down through every item below it, showing authority as a visible chain reaction instead of a claim.

title: Universal access spreads into a background grid
why: 'Everyone' becomes a grid you can count, and success for all becomes a wave sweeping across it, so scale is seen and not just quoted.

title: Identical success cards turn into a working product
why: A crowd of identical success markers becomes distinct named people doing varied work, and the viewer slides into one of them with no cut.

title: Opening promise becomes a measured time saving
why: A spoken line shown as an object held inside a machine feels like a pledge awaiting its test, not a title card.

title: Naming the problem amid tool clutter and live typing
why: Giving one phrase the full frame plus a focus pulse marks it as the film's central diagnosis, not just another narrated line.

title: Mounting clutter resolves into the brand
why: Consequences visibly stack up beside the sentence, so everything else turns into an amount the viewer has already watched grow, not an assertion.

title: Agent work scrolls into a real architecture canvas
why: Nobody can read it all and nobody needs to: the sheer quantity and variety of automated activity streaming by implies serious engineering took place.

title: Edits and agent actions form an auditable log
why: Each change is listed individually with undo beside it, so autonomy feels controlled, like a ledger of reversible transactions rather than a risk.

title: Brand name surrounded by real generated output
why: Content converges on the logo while everything else keeps moving, making the name the fixed center and the destination of all that is shown.

title: Typing a request and browsing the options
why: Typed text and a smoothly eased cursor with no click animation convince viewers a person is driving a real app, so what follows reads as its response.

title: Returning the pick and confirming the action
why: A single object carries the selection from the browsing layer into the form, so the viewer can follow what changed without explanatory text.

title: Product enters, states its promise, then leaves
